16--- program transformation: the `optimize0plus` function. The programming
17--- language we were considering was the first version of the language of

19--- very easy to define what it means for a program transformation to be
20--- correct: it should always yield a program that evaluates to the same number
21--- as the original.

25--- mutable state and develop a more sophisticated notion of correctness, which
26--- we'll call *behavioral equivalence*.
27-
28--- For example:
29-
30--- - `X + 2` is behaviorally equivalent to `1 + X + 1`
31--- - `X - X` is behaviorally equivalent to `0`
32--- - `(X - 1) + 1` is *not* behaviorally equivalent to `X`

13+--  ## Behavioral Equivaleence
14+
15+--  In an earlier chapter, we investigated the correctness of a very simple
16+--  program transformation: the `optimize0plus` function. The programming
17+--  language we were considering was the first version of the language of
18+--  arithmetic expressions -- with no variables -- so in that setting it
19+--  was very easy to define what it means for a program transformation to
20+--  be correct: it should always yield a program that evaluates to the same
21+--  number as the original.
22+
23+--  To talk about the correctness of program transformations for the full
24+--  Imp language -- in particular, assignment -- we need to consider the
25+--  role of mutable state and develop a more sophisticated notion of
26+--  correctness, which we'll call *behavioral equivalence*.
27+
28+--  For example:
29+
30+--  - `X + 2` is behaviorally equivalent to `1 + X + 1`
31+--  - `X - X` is behaviorally equivalent to `0`
32+--  - `(X - 1) + 1` is *not* behaviorally equivalent to `X`
33+
34+--  ### Definitions
35+
36+--  For `aexp`s and `bexp`s with variables, the definition we want is
37+--  clear: Two `aexp`s or `bexp`s are "behaviorally equivalent" if they
38+--  evaluate to the same result in every state.
3939

4141   ∀ (st : State),

5252     b₁.Equiv b₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st := by rfl

71--- For commands, the situation is a little more subtle. We can't simply say
72--- "two commands are behaviorally equivalent if they evaluate to the same
73--- ending state whenever they are started in the same initial state," because
74--- some commands, when run in some starting states, don't terminate in any
75--- final state at all!
76-
77--- What we need instead is this: two commands are behaviorally equivalent if,
78--- for any given starting state, they either (1) both diverge or else (2) both
79--- terminate in the same final state. A compact way to express this is "if the
80--- first one terminates in a particular state then so does the second, and
81--- vice versa."
71+--  For commands, the situation is a little more subtle. We can't simply
72+--  say "two commands are behaviorally equivalent if they evaluate to the
73+--  same ending state whenever they are started in the same initial state,"
74+--  because some commands, when run in some starting states, don't
75+--  terminate in any final state at all!
76+
77+--  What we need instead is this: two commands are behaviorally equivalent
78+--  if, for any given starting state, they either (1) both diverge or else
79+--  (2) both terminate in the same final state. A compact way to express
80+--  this is "if the first one terminates in a particular state then so does
81+--  the second, and vice versa."

239+--  To prove the second fact, we need an auxiliary lemma stating that

242+--  *Lemma*: If `b` is equivalent to `true`, then it cannot be the case

244+
245+--  *Proof*: Suppose that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. We show, by
246+--  induction on a derivation of `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`, that this
247+--  assumption leads to a contradiction. The only two cases to consider are
248+--  `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` and `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`; the others are
249+--  contradictory.
250+
251+--  - Suppose `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` is proved using rule
252+--    `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`. Then by assumption `b.eval st = false`. But
253+--    this contradicts the assumption that `b` is equivalent to `true`.
254+
255+--  - Suppose `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` is proved using rule
256+--    `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`. We must have:
257+
258+--    1. `b.eval st = true`, and
259+
260+--    2. there is some `st₀` such that `st =[ c ] => st₀` and
261+--       `st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`.
262+
263+--    3. Also, we are given an induction hypothesis saying that
264+--       `st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` leads to a contradiction,
265+
266+--    We obtain a contradiction by 2 and 3.

417--- ### Behavioral Equivalence is a Congruence
418-
419--- Less obviously, behavioral equivalence is also a *congruence*. That is, the
420--- equivalence of two subprograms implies the equivalence of the larger
421--- programs in which they are embedded:
422-
423--- aequiv a a' ------------------------- cequiv (x := a) (x := a')
424-
425--- cequiv c1 c1' cequiv c2 c2' -------------------------- cequiv (c1;c2)
426--- (c1';c2')
427-
428--- ... and so on for the other forms of commands.
429-
430--- (Note that we are using the inference rule notation here not as part of an
431--- inductive definition, but simply to write down some valid implications in a
432--- readable format. We prove these implications below.)
433-
434--- We will see a concrete example of why these congruence properties are
435--- important in the following section (in the proof of
436--- `fold_constants_com_sound`), but the main idea is that they allow us to
437--- replace a small part of a large program with an equivalent small part and
438--- know that the whole large programs are equivalent *without* doing an
439--- explicit proof about the parts that didn't change -- i.e., the "proof
440--- burden" of a small change to a large program is proportional to the size of
441--- the change, not the program!
422+--  ### Behavioral Equivalence is a Congruence
423+
424+--  Less obviously, behavioral equivalence is also a *congruence*. That is,
425+--  the equivalence of two subprograms implies the equivalence of the
426+--  larger programs in which they are embedded:
427+
428+--  aequiv a a' ------------------------- cequiv (x := a) (x := a')
429+
430+--  cequiv c1 c1' cequiv c2 c2' -------------------------- cequiv (c1;c2)
431+--  (c1';c2')
432+
433+--  ... and so on for the other forms of commands.
434+
435+--  (Note that we are using the inference rule notation here not as part of
436+--  an inductive definition, but simply to write down some valid
437+--  implications in a readable format. We prove these implications below.)
438+
439+--  We will see a concrete example of why these congruence properties are
440+--  important in the following section (in the proof of
441+--  `fold_constants_com_sound`), but the main idea is that they allow us to
442+--  replace a small part of a large program with an equivalent small part
443+--  and know that the whole large programs are equivalent *without* doing
444+--  an explicit proof about the parts that didn't change -- i.e., the
445+--  "proof burden" of a small change to a large program is proportional to
446+--  the size of the change, not the program!
442447 
443448 theorem Com.congruence.asgn {x : Ident} {a a' : Aexp} (ha : a.Equiv a') :
444449     (imp {x := ~a}).Equiv
454459       rw [Aexp.equiv_def] at ha
455460       rw [ha]
456461

460--- *Theorem*: Equivalence is a congruence for `while` -- that is, if `b` is
461--- equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to `c'`, then `while (~b) {~c}` is
462--- equivalent to `while (~b') {~c'}`.
463-
464--- *Proof*: Suppose `b` is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to `c'`.
465--- We must show, for every `st` and `st'`, that
466--- `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` iff `st = while (~b') {~c'}
467--- ]=> st'`. We
468--- consider the two directions separately.
469-
470--- - (`->`) We show that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` implies
471---   `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, by induction on a derivation of
472---   `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. The only nontrivial cases are when the
473---   final rule in the derivation is `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` or
474---   `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`.
475-
476---   - `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`: In this case, the form of the rule gives us
477---     `beval st b = false` and `st = st'`. But then, since `b` and `b'` are
478---     equivalent, we have `beval st b' =false`, and `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`
479---     applies, giving us `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, as required.
480-
481---   - `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`: The form of the rule now gives us
482---     `beval st b = true`, with `st =[ c ]=> st'0` and
483---     `st'0 =[ while {~b} {~c} ]=> st'` for some state `st'0`, with the induction
484---     hypothesis `st'0 =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`.
485-
486---     Since `c` and `c'` are equivalent, we know that `st =[ c']=> st'0`. And
487---     since `b` and `b'` are equivalent, we have `beval st b' = true`. Now
488---     `Com.EvalR.whileTrue` applies, giving us `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`,
489---     as required.
490-
491--- - (`<-`) Similar.
492-
462+--  The congruence property for loops is a little more interesting, since
463+--  it requires induction.
464+
465+--  *Theorem*: Equivalence is a congruence for `while` -- that is, if `b`
466+--  is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to `c'`, then
467+--  `while (~b) {~c}` is equivalent to `while (~b') {~c'}`.
468+
469+--  *Proof*: Suppose `b` is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to
470+--  `c'`. We must show, for every `st` and `st'`, that
471+--  `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` iff `st = while (~b') {~c'}
472+--  ]=> st'`.
473+--  We consider the two directions separately.
474+
475+--  - (`->`) We show that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` implies
476+--    `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, by induction on a derivation of
477+--    `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. The only nontrivial cases are when
478+--    the final rule in the derivation is `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` or
479+--    `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`.
480+
481+--    - `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`: In this case, the form of the rule gives us
482+--      `beval st b = false` and `st = st'`. But then, since `b` and `b'`
483+--      are equivalent, we have `beval st b' =false`, and
484+--      `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` applies, giving us
485+--      `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, as required.
486+
487+--    - `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`: The form of the rule now gives us
488+--      `beval st b = true`, with `st =[ c ]=> st'0` and
489+--      `st'0 =[ while {~b} {~c} ]=> st'` for some state `st'0`, with the
490+--      induction hypothesis `st'0 =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`.
491+
492+--      Since `c` and `c'` are equivalent, we know that `st =[ c']=> st'0`.
493+--      And since `b` and `b'` are equivalent, we have
494+--      `beval st b' = true`. Now `Com.EvalR.whileTrue` applies, giving us
495+--      `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, as required.
496+
497+--  - (`<-`) Similar.
498+

6--- # Hoare: Hoare Logic, Part I
7-
8--- In an earlier chapter, we began applying the mathematical tools developed
9--- in the first part of the course to studying the theory of a small
10--- programming language, Imp.
11-
12--- - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with an
13---   *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that specifies the
14---   *operational semantics* of programs.
15-
16---   The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key features of
17---   full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the fundamental
18---   notion of mutable state and some common control structures.
19-
20--- - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the sense
21---   that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather than of
22---   particular programs in the language. These included:
23-
24---   - determinism of evaluation
25-
26---   - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions (e.g.,
27---     functional and relational definitions of arithmetic expression evaluation)
28-
29---   - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
30-
31---   - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of useful
32---     program transformations
33-
34---   - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the Equiv chapter).
35-
36--- If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of tools
37--- for defining and discussing programming languages and language features
38--- that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work with, applied
39--- to a set of key properties. All of these properties are things that
40--- language designers, compiler writers, and users might care about knowing.
41--- Indeed, many of them are so fundamental to our understanding of the
42--- programming languages we deal with that we might not consciously recognize
43--- them as "theorems." But properties that seem intuitively obvious can
44--- sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also subtly wrong!).
45-
46--- In another volume of this series (*Type Systems*), we expand upon the theme
47--- of metatheoretic properties of whole languages when we discuss *types* and
48--- *type soundness*. In this chapter, though, we turn to a different set of
49--- issues.
50-
51--- Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work through some
52--- simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
53--- definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
54--- particular specifications of their behavior.
55-
56--- We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic* -- often
57--- shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of the syntactic
58--- constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be used
59--- to reason compositionally about the correctness of programs involving this
60--- construct.
61-
62--- Hoare Logic originated in the 1960s, and it continues to be the subject of
63--- intensive research right up to the present day. It lies at the core of a
64--- multitude of tools that are being used in academia and industry to specify
65--- and verify real software systems.
66-
67--- Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of writing down
68--- *specifications* of programs, and a *structured proof technique* for
69--- proving that programs are correct with respect to such specifications --
70--- where by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs directly mirrors
71--- the structure of the programs that they are about.
72-
73--- ## Assertions
74-
75--- An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a program's memory --
76--- formally, a predicate of `State`s.
6+--  # Hoare: Hoare Logic, Part I
7+
8+--  In an earlier chapter, we began applying the mathematical tools
9+--  developed in the first part of the course to studying the theory of a
10+--  small programming language, Imp.
11+
12+--  - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with
13+--    an *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that
14+--    specifies the *operational semantics* of programs.
15+
16+--    The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key
17+--    features of full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the
18+--    fundamental notion of mutable state and some common control
19+--    structures.
20+
21+--  - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the
22+--    sense that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather
23+--    than of particular programs in the language. These included:
24+
25+--    - determinism of evaluation
26+
27+--    - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions
28+--      (e.g., functional and relational definitions of arithmetic
29+--      expression evaluation)
30+
31+--    - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
32+
33+--    - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of
34+--      useful program transformations
35+
36+--    - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the Equiv chapter).
37+
38+--  If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of
39+--  tools for defining and discussing programming languages and language
40+--  features that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work
41+--  with, applied to a set of key properties. All of these properties are
42+--  things that language designers, compiler writers, and users might care
43+--  about knowing. Indeed, many of them are so fundamental to our
44+--  understanding of the programming languages we deal with that we might
45+--  not consciously recognize them as "theorems." But properties that seem
46+--  intuitively obvious can sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also
47+--  subtly wrong!).
48+
49+--  In another volume of this series (*Type Systems*), we expand upon the
50+--  theme of metatheoretic properties of whole languages when we discuss
51+--  *types* and *type soundness*. In this chapter, though, we turn to a
52+--  different set of issues.
53+
54+--  Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work through some
55+--  simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
56+--  definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
57+--  particular specifications of their behavior.
58+
59+--  We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic* -- often
60+--  shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of the syntactic
61+--  constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be
62+--  used to reason compositionally about the correctness of programs
63+--  involving this construct.
64+
65+--  Hoare Logic originated in the 1960s, and it continues to be the subject
66+--  of intensive research right up to the present day. It lies at the core
67+--  of a multitude of tools that are being used in academia and industry to
68+--  specify and verify real software systems.
69+
70+--  Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of writing down
71+--  *specifications* of programs, and a *structured proof technique* for
72+--  proving that programs are correct with respect to such specifications
73+--  -- where by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs directly
74+--  mirrors the structure of the programs that they are about.
75+
76+--  ## Assertions
77+
78+--  An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a program's memory
79+--  -- formally, a predicate of `State`s.

117--- ### Notations for Assertions
118-
119--- This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two reasons:
120--- (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to begin with
121--- `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that we ever use to
122--- look up variables in assertions (we will almost never need to talk about
123--- two different memory states at the same time). For discussing examples
124--- informally, we'll adopt some simplifying conventions: we'll drop the
125--- initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus,
126--- instead of writing
127-
128---   fun st => st[X] = m
129-
130--- we'll write just
131-
132---   {{ X = m }}.
133-
134--- Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
135--- assertion. We'll see more examples below.
136-
137--- This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout the
138--- Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like `X`,
139--- `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`, `y`, `m`,
140--- and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is why, when
141--- translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with `st[X]` but leave
142--- `m` alone.
143-
144--- The convention described above can be implemented with a little syntax
145--- magic, using coercions and a custom grammar, much as we did with the
146--- `imp { … }` notation in Imp. This new notation automatically lifts `Aexp`s,
147--- numbers, and `Prop`s into `Assertion`s when they appear between the
148--- `{{ _ }}` brackets, or when Lean knows that the type of an expression is
149--- `Assertion`.
150-
151--- There is no need to understand the details of how these notations work.
123+--  ### Notations for Assertions
124+
125+--  This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two
126+--  reasons: (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to
127+--  begin with `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that
128+--  we ever use to look up variables in assertions (we will almost never
129+--  need to talk about two different memory states at the same time). For
130+--  discussing examples informally, we'll adopt some simplifying
131+--  conventions: we'll drop the initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just
132+--  `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus, instead of writing
133+
134+--    fun st => st[X] = m
135+
136+--  we'll write just
137+
138+--    {{ X = m }}.
139+
140+--  Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
141+--  assertion. We'll see more examples below.
142+
143+--  This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout
144+--  the Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like
145+--  `X`, `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`,
146+--  `y`, `m`, and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is
147+--  why, when translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with
148+--  `st[X]` but leave `m` alone.
149+
150+--  The convention described above can be implemented with a little syntax
151+--  magic, using coercions and a custom grammar, much as we did with the
152+--  `imp { … }` notation in Imp. This new notation automatically lifts
153+--  `Aexp`s, numbers, and `Prop`s into `Assertion`s when they appear
154+--  between the `{{ _ }}` brackets, or when Lean knows that the type of an
155+--  expression is `Assertion`.
156+
157+--  There is no need to understand the details of how these notations work.

241--- Function applications inside assertions automatically interpret their
242--- arguments in the current state. Thus, `{{ f e1 ... en }}` stands for
243--- `fun st => f (e1 st) ... (en st)`.
244-
245--- Occasionally it is simpler to write an assertion directly as a Lean
246--- function. Such a function can be placed inside the assertion notation
247--- without an escape marker.
248-
249--- For example, `{{ fun st => ∀ x, st[x] = 0 }}` indicates an assertion that
250--- every variable maps to `0` in the given state.

279--- ### Printing Assertions
280-
281--- As in the Imp chapter, the assertion notation above is *input* only: Lean
282--- reads `{{ X ≤ 5 }}` but still prints the underlying function, as
283--- `#print assertion8` just showed. The delaborators below close the loop for
284--- plain assertions: a state lambda whose body Lean can rebuild is printed
285--- back in `{{ … }}` notation, and an assertion Lean cannot rebuild falls back
286--- to the raw `fun st => …` form, which is exactly this notation's escape
287--- syntax, so what you see is always valid input. Each time a new notation
288--- involving assertions appears below (implication, Hoare triples,
289--- substitution), a small delaborator defined next to it will extend this
290--- printing to cover it. As before, there is no need to understand the
291--- details.

404+--  ### Assertion Implication
405+
406+--  Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`,
407+--  written `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also
408+--  holds.

399411   ∀ st, P st → Q st

445--- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
446-
447--- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
448--- command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in this
449--- book, is
450-
451---   {{P}} c {{Q}}
452-
453--- meaning:
454-
455--- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
456--- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
457--- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
458-
459--- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
460--- *postcondition*.
461-
462--- For example,
463-
464--- - The Hoare triple
465-
466---   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
467-
468--- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
469--- a state in which `X = 1`.
470-
471--- - On the other hand,
472-
473---   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
474-
475--- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
476--- `{{X = m}} X :=
477--- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
478--- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
479--- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
480-
481--- _Quiz:_
482-
483--- Paraphrase the following in English.
484-
485---   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
486-
487---   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
488-
489---   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
490-
491---   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
492-
493---   5) ∀ m,
494---        {{X = m}}
495---        c
496---        {{Y = real_fact m}}
497-
498---   6) ∀ m,
499---        {{X = m}}
500---        c
501---        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
502-

506--- between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
507-
508---   {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
509-
510--- (A) Yes
511-
512--- (B) No
513-

517-

531-

456+
457+--  ## Hoare Triples, Informally
458+
459+--  A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing
460+--  a command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in
461+--  this book, is
462+
463+--    {{P}} c {{Q}}
464+
465+--  meaning:
466+
467+--  - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
468+--  - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
469+--  - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
470+
471+--  Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is
472+--  the *postcondition*.
473+
474+--  For example,
475+
476+--  - The Hoare triple
477+
478+--    {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
479+
480+--  states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which
481+--  `X = 0` to a state in which `X = 1`.
482+
483+--  - On the other hand,
484+
485+--    ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
486+
487+--  is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
488+--  `{{X = m}} X :=
489+--  X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`.
490+--  Note that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean*
491+--  variable `m`, which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
492+
493+--  _Quiz:_

496+
497+--    1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}

499+--    2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
500+
501+--    3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
502+
503+--    4) {{True}} c {{False}}
504+
505+--    5) ∀ m,
506+--         {{X = m}}
507+--         c
508+--         {{Y = real_fact m}}
509+
510+--    6) ∀ m,
511+--         {{X = m}}
512+--         c
513+--         {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
514+
515+--  _Quiz:_

517+--  Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the claimed relation
518+--  between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
519+
520+--    {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
521+
522+--  (A) Yes
523+
524+--  (B) No
525+
526+--  _Quiz:_
527+
528+--  What about this one?
529+
530+--    {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
531+
532+--  (A) Yes
533+
534+--  (B) No
535+
536+--  _Quiz:_

538+--  What about this one?
539+
540+--    {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
541+
542+--  (A) Yes
543+
544+--  (B) No
545+
546+--  _Quiz:_

548+--  What about this one?
549+
550+--    {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
551+
552+--  (A) Yes
553+
554+--  (B) No
555+
556+--  _Quiz:_

558+--  What about this one?

561+
562+--  (A) Yes

566+--  _Quiz:_

573+
574+--  (B) No
575+

712--- ## Proof Rules
713-
714--- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
715--- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
716--- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
717--- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
718--- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
719--- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
720--- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
721--- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
722--- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
723-
724--- ### Skip
725-
726--- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
727-
728---   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
729---   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
720+--  ## Proof Rules
721+
722+--  The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for
723+--  proving the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the
724+--  structure of a program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of
725+--  the program itself. To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce
726+--  a rule for reasoning about each of the different syntactic forms of
727+--  commands in Imp -- one for assignment, one for sequencing, one for
728+--  conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple of "structural" rules for gluing
729+--  things together. We will then be able to prove programs correct using
730+--  these proof rules, without ever unfolding the definition of
731+--  `ValidHoareTriple`.
732+
733+--  ### Skip
734+
735+--  Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
736+
737+--    --------------------  (hoare_skip)
738+--    {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
730739 
731740 theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
732741     {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
735744   inversion h
736745   exact hpre
737746 
738--- ### Sequencing
739-
740--- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
741--- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
742--- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
743--- where `R` holds:
744-
745---    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
746---    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
747---   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
748---   {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
747+--  ### Sequencing
748+
749+--  If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q`
750+--  holds, and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R`
751+--  holds, then doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P`
752+--  holds to one where `R` holds:
753+
754+--     {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
755+--     {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
756+--    ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
757+--    {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
749758 
750759 theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
751760     (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
757766     rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
758767     exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
759768 
760--- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
761--- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
762--- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
763--- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
764--- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
765--- through commands until we reach the beginning.
766-
767--- ### Assignment
768-
769--- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
770--- rules. Here's how it works.
771-

775-
776--- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
777--- could the precondition be?
778-
779--- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
780--- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
781-
782---   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
783-

785--- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
786--- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
787--- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
788--- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
789-
790--- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
791-
792---   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
793-
794--- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
795--- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:

797---   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
798-

802--- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
803--- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
804--- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
805--- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.

769+--  Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
770+--  backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
771+--  information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since
772+--  the natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end

775+
776+--  ### Assignment
777+
778+--  The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic
779+--  proof rules. Here's how it works.
780+
781+--  Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
782+
783+--    {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
784+
785+--  We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`.
786+--  What could the precondition be?
787+
788+--  One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then
789+--  assigning it to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare
790+--  triple:
791+
792+--    {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
793+
794+--  It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken
795+--  some clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done
796+--  it: if we take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with
797+--  `Y`---that is, replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement
798+--  with the right-hand side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
799+
800+--  That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
801+
802+--    {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
803+
804+--  If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
805+--  again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
806+
807+--    {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
808+
809+--  Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some
810+--  property `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned.
811+--  In this case, `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it
812+--  valid, we need to identify a precondition that guarantees that property
813+--  will hold of `X`. Such a precondition must ensure that the same
814+--  property holds of *whatever is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the
815+--  example, we need "equals `1`" to hold of `X + Y`. That's exactly what
816+--  the technique guarantees.
817+
818+--  In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`,
819+--  and the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary
820+--  arithmetic expression `a`:
821+
822+--    {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
823+
824+--  The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in
825+--  it replaced by `a`.
826+
827+--  Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences:
828+--  Define `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of
829+--  `X`".
830+
831+--  This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
832+
833+--    {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
834+
835+--  One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
836+--  terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
837+--  start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is
838+--  substituted for every occurrence of `X`.
839+
840+--  To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it
841+--  proceeds from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes
842+--  good sense to go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is
843+--  more important, because it characterizes what will be true after
844+--  running the code.
845+
846+--  Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment
847+--  rule. We'll do that later in some exercises.
848+
849+--  Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
850+
851+--    {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
852+--      X := X + 1
853+--    {{ X ≤ 5 }}
854+
855+--    {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
856+--      X := 3
857+--    {{ X = 3 }}
858+
859+--    {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
860+--      X := 3
861+--    {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
862+
863+--  To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of
864+--  "substituting an expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which
865+--  we refer to as assertion substitution, or `Assertion.subst`.
866+
867+--  Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
868+--  expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just
869+--  the same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P`
870+--  mentions `X`.
871+
872+--  This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions
873+--  for Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends).
874+--  The difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we
875+--  can't directly "edit" its text.
876+
877+--  However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated

938+
939+--  That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` --
940+--  that behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the
941+--  variable `X` in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the
942+--  expression `a`.
943+
944+--  To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with
945+--  a couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that
946+--  is, more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
947+
948+--    fun st =>
949+--      (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
950+--      (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
951+
952+--  which simplifies to
953+
954+--    fun st =>
955+--      (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
956+--      (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
957+
958+--  and further simplifies to
959+
960+--    fun st =>
961+--      ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
962+
963+--  and finally to
964+
965+--    fun st =>
966+--      3 ≤ 5.
967+
968+--  That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5`
969+--  (as expected).
970+
971+--  For a more interesting example, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦
972+--  X + 1]`.
973+--  Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
974+
975+--    fun st =>
976+--      (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
977+--      (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
978+
979+--  which simplifies to
980+
981+--    fun st =>
982+--      (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
983+
984+--  and further simplifies to
985+
986+--    fun st =>
987+--      (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
988+
989+--  That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.
990+

1133--- won't quite be the ones we want in the particular situation at hand -- they
1134--- may be logically equivalent but have a different syntactic form that fails
1135--- to unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they actually may be
1136--- logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for postconditions) than
1137--- what we need.
1138-

1146-
1147--- does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of `hoare_asgn`
1148--- because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not syntactically equal

1149+--  ### Consequence
1150+
1151+--  Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from the Hoare
1152+--  rules won't quite be the ones we want in the particular situation at
1153+--  hand -- they may be logically equivalent but have a different syntactic
1154+--  form that fails to unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they
1155+--  actually may be logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for
1156+--  postconditions) than what we need.
1157+
1158+--  For instance,
1159+
1160+--    {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1161+
1162+--  follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1163+
1164+--    {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1165+
1166+--  does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of
1167+--  `hoare_asgn` because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not
1168+--  syntactically equal assertions.
1169+
1170+--  However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple is valid,
1171+--  then the other must certainly be as well. We can capture this
1172+--  observation with the following rule:
1173+
1174+--       {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1175+--         P <<->> P'
1176+--    ---------------------
1177+--       {{P}} c {{Q}}
1178+
1179+--  Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that
1180+--  strengthening the precondition or weakening the postcondition of a
1181+--  valid triple always produces another valid triple. This observation is
1182+--  captured by two *Rules of Consequence*.
1183+
1184+--           {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1185+--              P ->> P'
1186+--    -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence_pre)
1187+--           {{P}} c {{Q}}
1188+
1189+--           {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1190+--             Q' ->> Q
1191+--    -----------------------------    (hoare_consequence_post)
1192+--           {{P}} c {{Q}}
1193+
1194+--  Here are the formal versions:

11771196 theorem hoare_consequence_pre {P P' Q : Assertion} {c : Com}
11781197     (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
11921211   apply himp
11931212   exact hhoare heval hpre
11941213

12451264   · exact hoare_consequence_post htriple hpost

1250--- Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare triples can be
1251--- streamlined using the automation techniques that we introduced in the
1252--- *Automation* chapter of *Logical Foundations*.
1253-
1254--- Recall that `simp` rewrites with any lemmas we pass it. The definitions
1255--- whose meaning we keep needing to expose in this chapter --
1256--- `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`, and `Assertion.subst` -- each come
1257--- with a characterizing lemma (`validHoareTriple_def`, `assertImplies_def`,
1258--- `Assertion.subst_def`) restating the definition as an equation. Passing
1259--- these lemmas to `simp` replaces the defined notions by their meanings
1260--- wherever they appear. We'll do that explicitly below (and shortly package
1261--- the recipe up as a tactic of our own).

1559+--  ### Conditionals
1560+
1561+--  What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional commands?
1562+
1563+--  Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing either of
1564+--  the branches, then it holds after the whole conditional. So we might be
1565+--  tempted to write:
1566+
1567+--            {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1568+--            {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1569+--    ---------------------------------
1570+--    {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1571+
1572+--  However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule, we cannot
1573+--  show
1574+
1575+--    {{ True }}
1576+--      if X = 0
1577+--        then Y := 2
1578+--        else Y := X + 1
1579+--      end
1580+--    {{ X ≤ Y }}
1581+
1582+--  since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in which the
1583+--  assignments take place in the "then" and "else" branches.
1584+
1585+--  Fortunately, we can say something more precise. In the "then" branch,
1586+--  we know that the boolean expression `b` evaluates to `true`, and in the
1587+--  "else" branch, we know it evaluates to `false`. Making this information
1588+--  available in the premises of the rule gives us more information to work
1589+--  with when reasoning about the behavior of `c1` and `c2` (i.e., the
1590+--  reasons why they establish the postcondition `Q`).
1591+
1592+--    {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1593+--    {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1594+--    ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1595+--    {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}

1891+--  ### While Loops
1892+
1893+--  The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of a *command
1894+--  invariant* (or just *invariant*): an assertion whose truth is
1895+--  guaranteed after executing a command, assuming it is true before.
1896+
1897+--  That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c` if
1898+
1899+--    {{P}} c {{P}}
1900+
1901+--  holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily become false
1902+--  in the middle of executing `c`, but by the end of `c` it must be
1903+--  restored.
1904+
1905+--  As a first attempt at a `while` rule, we could try:
18941906 
18951907 --           {{P}} c {{P}}
1896---   ---------------------------------
1897---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
1898-
1899--- Second, the loop body will be executed only if `b` is true. So we can also
1900--- strengthen the precondition in the premise:
1901-
1902---         {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1903---   --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
1904---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
1905-
1906--- That is the Hoare `while` rule. Note how it combines aspects of `skip` and
1907--- conditionals:
1908-
1909--- - If the loop body executes zero times, the rule is like `skip` in that the
1910---   precondition survives to become (part of) the postcondition.
1911-
1912--- - Like a conditional, we can assume guard `b` holds on entry to the
1913---   subcommand.
1908+--    ---------------------------
1909+--    {{P}} while b do c end {{P}}
1910+
1911+--  This rule is valid: if `P` is a command invariant of `c`, as the
1912+--  premise requires, then, no matter how many times the loop body
1913+--  executes, `P` is going to be true when the loop finally finishes.
1914+
1915+--  But the rule also omits two crucial pieces of information. First, the
1916+--  loop terminates when `b` becomes false. So we can strengthen the
1917+--  postcondition in the conclusion:
1918+
1919+--            {{P}} c {{P}}
1920+--    ---------------------------------
1921+--    {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
1922+
1923+--  Second, the loop body will be executed only if `b` is true. So we can
1924+--  also strengthen the precondition in the premise:
1925+
1926+--          {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1927+--    --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
1928+--    {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
1929+
1930+--  That is the Hoare `while` rule. Note how it combines aspects of `skip`
1931+--  and conditionals:
1932+
1933+--  - If the loop body executes zero times, the rule is like `skip` in that
1934+--    the precondition survives to become (part of) the postcondition.
1935+
1936+--  - Like a conditional, we can assume guard `b` holds on entry to the
1937+--    subcommand.
19141938 
19151939 theorem hoare_while {P : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
19161940     (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
19351959   | skip | asgn | seq | ifTrue | ifFalse =>
19361960     contradiction
19371961

2424--- ### Assert and Assume
2425-
2426--- In this exercise, we will extend IMP with two commands, `assert` and
2427--- `assume`. Both commands are ways to indicate that a certain assertion
2428--- should hold any time this part of the program is reached. However they
2429--- differ as follows:
2430-
2431--- - If an `assert` statement fails, it causes the program to go into an error
2432---   state and exit.
2433-
2434--- - If an `assume` statement fails, the program fails to evaluate at all. In
2435---   other words, the program gets stuck and has no final state.
2436-

2459+

2478--- an end state or to `error`. The `Result` type indicates the end value of a
2479--- program, either a state or an error:

2559+--  `Q`.

53--- ## Decorated Programs
54-
55--- The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the structure of
56--- proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
57-
58--- We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
59--- low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
60--- appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
61-
62--- Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its own
63--- correctness.
64-
65--- For example, consider the program:
66-
67---   X := m;
68---   Z := p;
69---   while X <> 0 do
70---     Z := Z - 1;
71---     X := X - 1
72---   end
73-
74--- Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a Hoare
75--- triple:
76-
77---   {{ True }}
78---   X := m;
79---   Z := p;
80---   while X <> 0 do
81---     Z := Z - 1;
82---     X := X - 1
83---   end
84---   {{ Z = p - m }}
85-
86--- (Note the *parameters* `m` and `p`, which stand for fixed-but-arbitrary
87--- numbers. Formally, they are simply Lean variables of type `Nat`.)
88-
89--- Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a proof of this
90--- specification:
91-
92---   {{ True }} ->>
93---   {{ m = m }}
94---     X := m
95---                        {{ X = m }} ->>
96---                        {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
97---     Z := p;
98---                        {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
99---                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
100---     while X <> 0 do
101---                        {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
102---                        {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
103---       Z := Z - 1
104---                        {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
105---       X := X - 1
106---                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
107---     end
108---   {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
109---   {{ Z = p - m }}
110-
111--- Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text interleaved
112--- with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by ->>).
113-
114--- A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a proof in
115--- Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify the Hoare
116--- triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of the Hoare
117--- Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows how to assemble
118--- all these individual steps into a proof for the whole program.
119-
120--- Our goal is to verify such decorated programs "mostly automatically." But,
121--- before we can verify anything, we need to be able to *find* a proof for a
122--- given specification, and for this we need to discover the right assertions.
123--- This can be done in an almost mechanical way, with the exception of finding
124--- loop invariants. In the remainder of this section, we explain in detail how
125--- to construct decorations for several short programs, all of which are loop
126--- free or have simple loop invariants. We'll return to finding more
127--- interesting loop invariants later in the chapter.
128-
129--- ### Example: Swapping
130-
131--- Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
132--- using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary
133--- variable.
134-
135---   X := X + Y;
136---   Y := X - Y;
137---   X := X - Y
138-
139--- We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
140--- correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
141-
142---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
143---   (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
144---            X := X + Y
145---   (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
146---            Y := X - Y
147---   (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
148---            X := X - Y
149---   (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
150-
151--- The decorations can be constructed as follows:
152-
153--- - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
154-
155--- - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
156---   postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n` to
157---   remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we can refer
158---   to them in the postcondition (5).
159-
160--- - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding until we
161---   get to (2). At each step, we obtain the precondition of the assignment from
162---   its postcondition by substituting the assigned variable with the
163---   right-hand-side of the assignment. For instance, we obtain (4) by
164---   substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3) by substituting `Y`
165---   with `X - Y` in (4).
166-
167--- - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the step
168---   from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by doing a bit
169---   of high-school algebra.
170-
171--- ### Example: Simple Conditionals
172-
173--- Here is a simple decorated program using conditionals:
174-
175---   (1)   {{ True }}
176---           if X <= Y then
177---   (2)                    {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
178---   (3)                    {{ (Y - X) + X = Y \/ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
179---             Z := Y - X
180---   (4)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
181---           else
182---   (5)                    {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
183---   (6)                    {{ (X - Y) + X = Y \/ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
184---             Z := X - Y
185---   (7)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
186---           end
187---   (8)   {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
188-
189--- These decorations can be constructed as follows:
190-
191--- - We start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (8).
192-
193--- - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_if` rule, we copy the
194---   postcondition (8) to (4) and (7). We conjoin the precondition (1) with the
195---   guard of the conditional to obtain (2). We conjoin (1) with the negated
196---   guard of the conditional to obtain (5).
197-
198--- - In order to use the assignment rule and obtain (3), we substitute `Z` by
199---   `Y - X` in (4). To obtain (6) we substitute `Z` by `X - Y` in (7).
200-
201--- - Finally, we verify that (2) implies (3) and (5) implies (6). Both of these
202---   implications crucially depend on the ordering of `X` and `Y` obtained from
203---   the guard. For instance, knowing that `X <= Y` ensures that subtracting `X`
204---   from `Y` and then adding back `X` produces `Y`, as required by the first
205---   disjunct of (3). Similarly, knowing that `~ (X <= Y)` ensures that
206---   subtracting `Y` from `X` and then adding back `Y` produces `X`, as needed
207---   by the second disjunct of (6). Note that `n - m + m = n` does *not* hold
208---   for arbitrary natural numbers `n` and `m` (for example, [3 - 5 + 5 = 5]).
209-

53+--  ## Decorated Programs
54+
55+--  The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the
56+--  structure of proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
57+
58+--  We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
59+--  low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
60+--  appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
61+
62+--  Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its
63+--  own correctness.
64+
65+--  For example, consider the program:
66+
67+--    X := m;
68+--    Z := p;
69+--    while X <> 0 do
70+--      Z := Z - 1;
71+--      X := X - 1
72+--    end
73+
74+--  Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a
75+--  Hoare triple:
76+
77+--    {{ True }}
78+--    X := m;
79+--    Z := p;
80+--    while X <> 0 do
81+--      Z := Z - 1;
82+--      X := X - 1
83+--    end
84+--    {{ Z = p - m }}
85+
86+--  (Note the *parameters* `m` and `p`, which stand for fixed-but-arbitrary
87+--  numbers. Formally, they are simply Lean variables of type `Nat`.)
88+
89+--  Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a proof of this
90+--  specification:
91+
92+--    {{ True }} ->>
93+--    {{ m = m }}
94+--      X := m
95+--                         {{ X = m }} ->>
96+--                         {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
97+--      Z := p;
98+--                         {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
99+--                         {{ Z - X = p - m }}
100+--      while X <> 0 do
101+--                         {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
102+--                         {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
103+--        Z := Z - 1
104+--                         {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
105+--        X := X - 1
106+--                         {{ Z - X = p - m }}
107+--      end
108+--    {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
109+--    {{ Z = p - m }}
110+
111+--  Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text
112+--  interleaved with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by
113+--  ->>).
114+
115+--  A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a
116+--  proof in Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify
117+--  the Hoare triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of
118+--  the Hoare Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows
119+--  how to assemble all these individual steps into a proof for the whole
120+--  program.
121+
122+--  Our goal is to verify such decorated programs "mostly automatically."
123+--  But, before we can verify anything, we need to be able to *find* a
124+--  proof for a given specification, and for this we need to discover the
125+--  right assertions. This can be done in an almost mechanical way, with
126+--  the exception of finding loop invariants. In the remainder of this
127+--  section, we explain in detail how to construct decorations for several
128+--  short programs, all of which are loop free or have simple loop
129+--  invariants. We'll return to finding more interesting loop invariants
130+--  later in the chapter.
131+
132+--  ### Example: Swapping
133+
134+--  Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
135+--  using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary
136+--  variable.
137+
138+--    X := X + Y;
139+--    Y := X - Y;
140+--    X := X - Y
141+
142+--  We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
143+--  correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
144+
145+--    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
146+--    (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
147+--             X := X + Y
148+--    (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
149+--             Y := X - Y
150+--    (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
151+--             X := X - Y
152+--    (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
153+
154+--  The decorations can be constructed as follows:
155+
156+--  - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
157+
158+--  - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
159+--    postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n`
160+--    to remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we
161+--    can refer to them in the postcondition (5).
162+
163+--  - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding
164+--    until we get to (2). At each step, we obtain the precondition of the
165+--    assignment from its postcondition by substituting the assigned
166+--    variable with the right-hand-side of the assignment. For instance, we
167+--    obtain (4) by substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3)
168+--    by substituting `Y` with `X - Y` in (4).
169+
170+--  - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the
171+--    step from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by
172+--    doing a bit of high-school algebra.
173+
174+--  ### Example: Simple Conditionals
175+
176+--  Here is a simple decorated program using conditionals:
177+

179+--            if X <= Y then
180+--    (2)                    {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
181+--    (3)                    {{ (Y - X) + X = Y \/ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
182+--              Z := Y - X
183+--    (4)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
184+--            else
185+--    (5)                    {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
186+--    (6)                    {{ (X - Y) + X = Y \/ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
187+--              Z := X - Y
188+--    (7)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
244189 --            end

246---   (6)    {{ X = 0 }}

237+--  ### Example: Reduce to Zero
238+
239+--  Here is a `while` loop that is so simple that `True` suffices as a loop
240+--  invariant.
241+
242+--    (1)    {{ True }}
243+--             while X <> 0 do
244+--    (2)                  {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
245+--    (3)                  {{ True }}
246+--               X := X - 1
247+--    (4)                  {{ True }}
248+--             end
249+--    (5)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>
250+--    (6)    {{ X = 0 }}
251+
252+--  The decorations can be constructed as follows:
253+
254+--  - Start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (6).
255+
256+--  - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_while` rule, we copy (1)
257+--    to (4). We conjoin (1) with the guard to obtain (2). We also conjoin
258+--    (1) with the negation of the guard to obtain (5).
259+
260+--  - Because the final postcondition (6) does not syntactically match (5),
261+--    we add an implication between them.
262+
263+--  - Using the assignment rule with assertion (4), we trivially substitute
264+--    and obtain assertion (3).
265+
266+--  - We add the implication between (2) and (3).
267+
268+--  Finally we check that the implications do hold; both are trivial.

270+--  ### Example: Division
271+
272+--  Let's do one more example of simple reasoning about a loop.
273+
274+--  The following Imp program calculates the integer quotient and remainder
275+--  of parameters `m` and `n`.
276+
277+--    X := m;
278+--    Y := 0;
279+--    while n <= X do
280+--      X := X - n;
281+--      Y := Y + 1
282+--    end;
283+
284+--  If we replace `m` and `n` by concrete numbers and execute the program,
285+--  it will terminate with the variable `X` set to the remainder when `m`
286+--  is divided by `n` and `Y` set to the quotient.
287+
288+--  In order to give a specification to this program we need to remember
289+--  that dividing `m` by `n` produces a remainder `X` and a quotient `Y`
290+--  such that `n * Y + X = m /\ X < n`.
291+
292+--  It turns out that we get lucky with this program and don't have to
293+--  think very hard about the loop invariant: the loop invariant is just
294+--  the first conjunct, `n * Y + X = m`, and we can use this to decorate
295+--  the program.
296+
297+--     (1)  {{ True }} ->>
298+--     (2)  {{ n * 0 + m = m }}
299+--            X := m;
300+--     (3)                     {{ n * 0 + X = m }}
301+--            Y := 0;
302+--     (4)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
303+--            while n <= X do
304+--     (5)                     {{ n * Y + X = m /\ n <= X }} ->>
305+--     (6)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + (X - n) = m }}
306+--              X := X - n;
307+--     (7)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + X = m }}
308+--              Y := Y + 1
309+--     (8)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
310+--            end
311+--     (9)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ ~ (n <= X) }} ->>
312+--    (10)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ X < n }}
313+
314+--  Assertions (4), (5), (8), and (9) are derived mechanically from the
315+--  loop invariant and the loop's guard. Assertions (8), (7), and (6) are
316+--  derived using the assignment rule going backwards from (8) to (6).
317+--  Assertions (4), (3), and (2) are again backwards applications of the
318+--  assignment rule.
319+
320+--  Now that we've decorated the program it only remains to check that the
321+--  uses of the consequence rule are correct — i.e., that (1) implies (2),
322+--  that (5) implies (6), and that (9) implies (10). This is indeed the
323+--  case:
324+
325+--  - (1) ->> (2): trivial, by algebra.
326+
327+--  - (5) ->> (6): because `n <= X`, we are guaranteed that the subtraction
328+--    in (6) does not get zero-truncated. We can therefore rewrite (6) as
329+--    `n * Y + n + X - n` and cancel the `n`s, which results in the left
330+--    conjunct of (5).
331+
332+--  - (9) ->> (10): if `~ (n <= X)` then `X < n`. That's straightforward
333+--    from high-school algebra. So, we have a valid decorated program.
334+

388+--  ## Formal Decorated Programs
389+
390+--  Our informal conventions for decorated programs amount to a way of
391+--  "displaying" Hoare triples, in which commands are annotated with enough
392+--  embedded assertions that checking the validity of a triple is reduced
393+--  to simple logical and algebraic calculations showing that some
394+--  assertions imply others.
395+
396+--  In this section, we show that this presentation style can be made
397+--  completely formal — and indeed that checking the validity of decorated
398+--  programs can be largely automated.
399+

404+--  "decorations." We call the new commands *decorated commands*, or
405+--  `dcom`s.
406+

445+
446+--  Instead, our formal syntax of decorated commands will omit
447+--  preconditions whenever possible and embed just postconditions.
448+
449+--  - The `skip` command, for example, is decorated only with its
450+--    postcondition
451+
452+--    skip {{ Q }}
453+
454+--  on the assumption that the precondition will be provided by somebody
455+--  else.
456+
457+--  We carry the same assumption through the other syntactic forms: each
458+--  decorated command is assumed to carry its own postcondition within
459+--  itself but take its precondition from its context in which it is used.
460+
461+--  - Sequences `d1 ; d2` need no additional decorations.
462+
463+--  Why?
464+
465+--  Because inside `d2` there will be a postcondition, which also serves as
466+--  the postcondition of `d1;d2`.
467+
468+--  Similarly, inside `d1` there will also be a postcondition, which
469+--  additionally serves as the *precondition* for `d2`.
470+
471+--  - An assignment `X := a` is decorated only with its postcondition:
472+
473+--    X := a {{ Q }}
474+
475+--  - A conditional `if b then d1 else d2` is decorated with a
476+--    postcondition for the entire statement, as well as preconditions for
477+--    each branch:
478+
479+--    if b then {{ P1 }} d1 else {{ P2 }} d2 end {{ Q }}
480+
481+--  - A loop `while b do d end` is decorated with its final postcondition
482+--    plus a precondition for the body:
483+
484+--    while b do {{ P }} d end {{ Q }}
485+
486+--  The postcondition embedded in `d` serves as the loop invariant.
487+
488+--  - Implications `->>` can be added as decorations either for a
489+--    precondition...
490+
491+--    ->> {{ P }} d
492+
493+--  ...or for a postcondition:
494+
495+--    d ->> {{ Q }}
496+
497+--  The former is waiting for another precondition to be supplied by the
498+--  context; the latter relies on the postcondition already embedded in
499+--  `d`.
500+
501+--  Putting this all together gives us the formal syntax of decorated
502+--  commands:
485503 
486504 inductive DCom where
487505   | skip (post : Assertion)
496514   | pre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
497515   | post (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
498516

682+--  The outer Hoare triple of a decorated program is just a `Prop`; thus,
683+--  to show that it is *valid*, we need to produce a proof of this
684+--  proposition.
685+
686+--  We will do this by extracting "proof obligations" from the decorations
687+--  sprinkled throughout the program.
688+
689+--  These obligations are often called *verification conditions*, because
690+--  they are the facts that must be verified to see that the decorations
691+--  are locally consistent and thus constitute a proof of validity of the
692+--  outer triple.
693+
694+--  ### Extracting Verification Conditions
695+
696+--  The function `DCom.VerificationConditions` takes a decorated command
697+--  `d` together with a precondition `P` and returns a *proposition* that,
698+--  if it can be proved, implies that the triple
699+
700+--    {{P}} d.erase {{d.postcondition}}
701+
702+--  is valid.
703+
704+--  It does this by walking over `d` and generating a big conjunction that
705+--  includes
706+
707+--  - local consistency checks for each form of command, plus
708+
709+--  - uses of `->>` to bridge the gap between the assertions found inside a
710+--    decorated command and the assertions imposed by the external
711+--    precondition; these uses correspond to applications of the
712+--    consequence rule.
713+
714+--  *Local consistency* is defined as follows...
715+
716+--  - The decorated command
717+
718+--    skip {{Q}}
719+
720+--  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if `P ->> Q`.
721+
722+--  - The sequential composition of `d1` and `d2` is locally consistent
723+--    with respect to `P` if `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
724+--    and `d2` is locally consistent with respect to the postcondition of
725+--    `d1`.
726+
727+--  - An assignment
728+
729+--    X := a {{Q}}
730+
731+--  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
732+
733+--    P ->> Q [X |-> a]
734+
735+--  - A conditional
736+
737+--    if b then {{P1}} d1 else {{P2}} d2 end {{Q}}
738+
739+--  is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if
740+
741+--  (1) `P /\ b ->> P1`
742+
743+--  (2) `P /\ ~b ->> P2`
744+
745+--  (3) `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P1`
746+
747+--  (4) `d2` is locally consistent with respect to `P2`
748+
749+--  (5) `d1.postcondition ->> Q`
750+
751+--  (6) `d2.postcondition ->> Q`
752+
753+--  - A loop
754+
755+--    while b do {{Q}} d end {{R}}
756+
757+--  is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if:
758+
759+--  (1) `P ->> d.postcondition`
760+
761+--  (2) `d.postcondition /\ b ->> Q`
762+
763+--  (3) `d.postcondition /\ ~b ->> R`
764+
765+--  (4) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
766+
767+--  - A command with an extra assertion at the beginning
768+
769+--    ->> {{Q}} d
770+
771+--  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
772+
773+--  (1) `P ->> Q`
774+
775+--  (2) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
776+
777+--  - A command with an extra assertion at the end
778+
779+--    d ->> {{Q}}
780+
781+--  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
782+
783+--  (1) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
784+
785+--  (2) `d.postcondition ->> Q`
786+
787+--  With all this in mind, we can write a *verification condition
788+--  generator* that takes a decorated command and reads off a proposition
789+--  saying that all its decorations are locally consistent.
790+
791+--  Formally, since a decorated command is "waiting for its precondition"
792+--  the main VC generator takes a `dcom` plus a given precondition as
793+--  arguments.
771794 
772795 def DCom.VerificationConditions
773796     (P : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
799822       body.VerificationConditions P ∧
800823       (body.postcondition ->> Q)
801824

946--- ## Finding Loop Invariants
947-
948--- Once the outermost precondition and postcondition are chosen, the only
949--- creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the right
950--- loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the reason
951--- that inductive mathematical proofs are:
952-
953--- - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger assumption
954---   to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of the loop body,
955---   but it also means that the loop body's postcondition is harder to prove.
956-
957--- - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you have a
958---   stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the induction step
959---   of the proof, but it also means that the statement being proved inductively
960---   is harder to prove.
961-
962--- This section explains how to approach the challenge of finding loop
963--- invariants through a series of examples and exercises.
964-
965--- ### Example: Slow Subtraction
966-
967--- The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the value of `Y` by
968--- repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We want to verify its correctness
969--- with respect to the pre- and postconditions shown:
970-
971---   {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
972---     while X <> 0 do
973---       Y := Y - 1;
974---       X := X - 1
975---     end
976---   {{ Y = n - m }}
977-
978--- To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv` for the loop. As
979--- a first step we can leave `Inv` as an unknown and build a *skeleton* for
980--- the proof by applying the rules for local consistency, working from the end
981--- of the program to the beginning, as usual, and without doing any thinking
982--- at all yet.
983-
984--- This leads to the following skeleton:
985-
986---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
987---   (2)    {{ Inv }}
988---            while X <> 0 do
989---   (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
990---   (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
991---              Y := Y - 1;
992---   (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
993---              X := X - 1
994---   (6)              {{ Inv }}
995---            end
996---   (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
997---   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
998-
999--- Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
1000--- respect three conditions:
1001-
1002--- - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's precondition,
1003---   i.e., (1) must imply (2);
1004-
1005--- - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's postcondition, i.e.,
1006---   (7) must imply (8);
1007-
1008--- - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the loop, assuming that
1009---   the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must imply (4).
1010-
1011--- These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
1012--- specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy them.
1013-
1014--- One way to find a loop invariant that simultaneously satisfies these three
1015--- conditions is by using an iterative process: start with a "candidate"
1016--- invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check the three
1017--- conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the information
1018--- that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully better —
1019--- candidate invariant, and repeat.
1020-
1021--- For instance, in the reduce-to-zero example above, we saw that, for a very
1022--- simple loop, choosing `True` as a loop invariant did the job. Maybe it will
1023--- work here too. To find out, let's try instantiating `Inv` with `True` in
1024--- the skeleton above and see what we get...
1025-
1026---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                    (a - OK)
1027---   (2)    {{ True }}
1028---            while X <> 0 do
1029---   (3)                   {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>     (c - OK)
1030---   (4)                   {{ True }}
1031---              Y := Y - 1;
1032---   (5)                   {{ True }}
1033---              X := X - 1
1034---   (6)                   {{ True }}
1035---            end
1036---   (7)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                 (b - WRONG!)
1037---   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1038-
1039--- While conditions (a) and (c) are trivially satisfied, (b) is wrong: it is
1040--- not the case that `True /\ X = 0` (7) implies `Y = n - m` (8). In fact, the
1041--- two assertions are completely unrelated, so it is very easy to find a
1042--- counterexample to the implication (say, `Y = X = m = 0` and `n = 1`).
1043-
1044--- If we want (b) to hold, we need to strengthen the loop invariant so that it
1045--- implies the postcondition (8). One simple way to do this is to let the loop
1046--- invariant *be* the postcondition. So let's return to our skeleton,
1047--- instantiate `Inv` with `Y = n - m`, and try checking conditions (a) to (c)
1048--- again.
1049-
1050---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                        (a - WRONG!)
1051---   (2)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1052---            while X <> 0 do
1053---   (3)                     {{ Y = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>  (c - WRONG!)
1054---   (4)                     {{ Y - 1 = n - m }}
1055---              Y := Y - 1;
1056---   (5)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1057---              X := X - 1
1058---   (6)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1059---            end
1060---   (7)    {{ Y = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1061---   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1062-
1063--- This time, condition (b) holds trivially, but (a) and (c) are broken.
1064--- Condition (a) requires that (1) `X = m /\ Y = n` implies (2) `Y = n - m`.
1065--- If we substitute `Y` by `n` we have to show that `n = n - m` for arbitrary
1066--- `m` and `n`, which is not the case (for instance, when `m = n = 1`).
1067--- Condition (c) requires that `n - m - 1 = n - m`, which fails, for instance,
1068--- for `n = 1` and `m = 0`. So, although `Y = n - m` holds at the end of the
1069--- loop, it does not hold from the start, and it doesn't hold on each
1070--- iteration; it is not a correct loop invariant.
1071-
1072--- This failure is not very surprising: the variable `Y` changes during the
