969+--  ## Finding Loop Invariants
970+
971+--  Once the outermost precondition and postcondition are chosen, the only
972+--  creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the
973+--  right loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the
974+--  reason that inductive mathematical proofs are:
975+
976+--  - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger
977+--    assumption to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of
978+--    the loop body, but it also means that the loop body's postcondition
979+--    is harder to prove.
980+
981+--  - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you
982+--    have a stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the
983+--    induction step of the proof, but it also means that the statement
984+--    being proved inductively is harder to prove.
985+
986+--  This section explains how to approach the challenge of finding loop
987+--  invariants through a series of examples and exercises.
988+
989+--  ### Example: Slow Subtraction
990+
991+--  The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the value of `Y`
992+--  by repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We want to verify its
993+--  correctness with respect to the pre- and postconditions shown:
994+
995+--    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
996+--      while X <> 0 do
997+--        Y := Y - 1;
998+--        X := X - 1
999+--      end
1000+--    {{ Y = n - m }}
1001+
1002+--  To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv` for the
1003+--  loop. As a first step we can leave `Inv` as an unknown and build a
1004+--  *skeleton* for the proof by applying the rules for local consistency,
1005+--  working from the end of the program to the beginning, as usual, and
1006+--  without doing any thinking at all yet.
1007+
1008+--  This leads to the following skeleton:
1009+
1010+--    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
1011+--    (2)    {{ Inv }}
1012+--             while X <> 0 do
1013+--    (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
1014+--    (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
1015+--               Y := Y - 1;
1016+--    (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
1017+--               X := X - 1
1018+--    (6)              {{ Inv }}
1019+--             end
1020+--    (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
1021+--    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1022+
1023+--  Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
1024+--  respect three conditions:
1025+
1026+--  - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's
1027+--    precondition, i.e., (1) must imply (2);
1028+
1029+--  - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's postcondition,
1030+--    i.e., (7) must imply (8);
1031+
1032+--  - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the loop,
1033+--    assuming that the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must
1034+--    imply (4).
1035+
1036+--  These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
1037+--  specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy
1038+--  them.
1039+
1040+--  One way to find a loop invariant that simultaneously satisfies these
1041+--  three conditions is by using an iterative process: start with a
1042+--  "candidate" invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check
1043+--  the three conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the
1044+--  information that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully
1045+--  better — candidate invariant, and repeat.
1046+
1047+--  For instance, in the reduce-to-zero example above, we saw that, for a
1048+--  very simple loop, choosing `True` as a loop invariant did the job.
1049+--  Maybe it will work here too. To find out, let's try instantiating `Inv`
1050+--  with `True` in the skeleton above and see what we get...
1051+
1052+--    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                    (a - OK)
1053+--    (2)    {{ True }}
1054+--             while X <> 0 do
1055+--    (3)                   {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>     (c - OK)
1056+--    (4)                   {{ True }}
1057+--               Y := Y - 1;
1058+--    (5)                   {{ True }}
1059+--               X := X - 1
1060+--    (6)                   {{ True }}
1061+--             end
1062+--    (7)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                 (b - WRONG!)
1063+--    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1064+
1065+--  While conditions (a) and (c) are trivially satisfied, (b) is wrong: it
1066+--  is not the case that `True /\ X = 0` (7) implies `Y = n - m` (8). In
1067+--  fact, the two assertions are completely unrelated, so it is very easy
1068+--  to find a counterexample to the implication (say, `Y = X = m = 0` and
1069+--  `n = 1`).
1070+
1071+--  If we want (b) to hold, we need to strengthen the loop invariant so
1072+--  that it implies the postcondition (8). One simple way to do this is to
1073+--  let the loop invariant *be* the postcondition. So let's return to our
1074+--  skeleton, instantiate `Inv` with `Y = n - m`, and try checking
1075+--  conditions (a) to (c) again.
1076+
1077+--    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                        (a - WRONG!)
1078+--    (2)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1079+--             while X <> 0 do
1080+--    (3)                     {{ Y = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>  (c - WRONG!)
1081+--    (4)                     {{ Y - 1 = n - m }}
1082+--               Y := Y - 1;
1083+--    (5)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1084+--               X := X - 1
1085+--    (6)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1086+--             end
1087+--    (7)    {{ Y = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1088+--    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1089+
1090+--  This time, condition (b) holds trivially, but (a) and (c) are broken.
1091+--  Condition (a) requires that (1) `X = m /\ Y = n` implies (2)
1092+--  `Y = n - m`. If we substitute `Y` by `n` we have to show that
1093+--  `n = n - m` for arbitrary `m` and `n`, which is not the case (for
1094+--  instance, when `m = n = 1`). Condition (c) requires that
1095+--  `n - m - 1 = n - m`, which fails, for instance, for `n = 1` and
1096+--  `m = 0`. So, although `Y = n - m` holds at the end of the loop, it does
1097+--  not hold from the start, and it doesn't hold on each iteration; it is
1098+--  not a correct loop invariant.
1099+
1100+--  This failure is not very surprising: the variable `Y` changes during
1101+--  the loop, while `m` and `n` are constant, so the assertion we chose
1102+--  didn't have much chance of being a loop invariant!
1103+
1104+--  To do better, we need to generalize (7) to some statement that is
1105+--  equivalent to (8) when `X` is `0`, since this will be the case when the
1106+--  loop terminates, and that "fills the gap" in some appropriate way when
1107+--  `X` is nonzero. Looking at how the loop works, we can observe that `X`
1108+--  and `Y` are decremented together until `X` reaches `0`. So, if `X = 2`
1109+--  and `Y = 5` initially, after one iteration of the loop we obtain
1110+--  `X = 1` and `Y = 4`; after two iterations `X = 0` and `Y = 3`; and then
1111+--  the loop stops. Notice that the difference between `Y` and `X` stays
1112+--  constant between iterations: initially, `Y = n` and `X = m`, and the
1113+--  difference is always `n - m`. So let's try instantiating `Inv` in the
1114+--  skeleton above with `Y - X = n - m`.
1115+
1116+--    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                            (a - OK)
1117+--    (2)    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1118+--             while X <> 0 do
1119+--    (3)                    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>   (c - OK)
1120+--    (4)                    {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1121+--               Y := Y - 1;
1122+--    (5)                    {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1123+--               X := X - 1
1124+--    (6)                    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1125+--             end
1126+--    (7)    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1127+--    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1128+
1129+--  Success! Conditions (a), (b) and (c) all hold now. (To verify (c), we
1130+--  need to check that, under the assumption that `X <> 0`, we have
1131+--  `Y - X = (Y - 1) - (X - 1)`; this holds for all natural numbers `X` and
1132+--  `Y`.)
1133+
1134+--  Here is the final version of the decorated program:
11061135 
11071136 def subtractSlowlyDec (m n : Nat) : Decorated where
11081137   pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
11221151     (subtractSlowlyDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by

1737--- ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
1738-
1739--- Some preconditions are more interesting than others. For example, the Hoare
1740--- triple
1741-
1742---   {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
1743-
1744--- is *not* very interesting: although it is perfectly valid, it tells us
1745--- nothing useful. Since the precondition isn't satisfied by any state, it
1746--- doesn't describe any situations where we can use the command `X := Y + 1`
1747--- to achieve the postcondition `X <= 5`.
1748-
1749--- By contrast,
1750-
1751---   {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
1752-
1753--- has a useful precondition: it tells us that, if we can somehow create a
1754--- situation in which we know that `Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0`, then running this
1755--- command will produce a state satisfying the postcondition. However, this
1756--- precondition is not as useful as it could be, because the `Z = 0` clause in
1757--- the precondition actually has nothing to do with the postcondition
1758--- `X <= 5`.
1759-
1760--- The *most* useful precondition for this command is this one:
1761-
1762---   {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
1763-
1764--- The assertion `Y <= 4` is called the *weakest precondition* of `X := Y + 1`
1765--- with respect to the postcondition `X <= 5`.
1766-
1767--- Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command `X := Y + 1` with
1768--- respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as meaning
1769--- "easiest to satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as many states as
1770--- possible can satisfy.
1771-
1772--- `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for postcondition `Q` if
1773-
1774--- - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
1775-
1776--- - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is, if
1777---   `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
1778-
1779--- Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For example, `Y <= 4`
1780--- was a weakest precondition above, but so are the logically equivalent
1781--- assertions `Y < 5`, `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show that any two
1782--- weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with respect to
1783--- postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is, `P <<->> P'`.
1768+--  ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
1769+
1770+--  Some preconditions are more interesting than others. For example, the
1771+--  Hoare triple
1772+
1773+--    {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
1774+
1775+--  is *not* very interesting: although it is perfectly valid, it tells us
1776+--  nothing useful. Since the precondition isn't satisfied by any state, it
1777+--  doesn't describe any situations where we can use the command
1778+--  `X := Y + 1` to achieve the postcondition `X <= 5`.
1779+
1780+--  By contrast,
1781+
1782+--    {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
1783+
1784+--  has a useful precondition: it tells us that, if we can somehow create a
1785+--  situation in which we know that `Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0`, then running this
1786+--  command will produce a state satisfying the postcondition. However,
1787+--  this precondition is not as useful as it could be, because the `Z = 0`
1788+--  clause in the precondition actually has nothing to do with the
1789+--  postcondition `X <= 5`.
1790+
1791+--  The *most* useful precondition for this command is this one:
1792+
1793+--    {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
1794+
1795+--  The assertion `Y <= 4` is called the *weakest precondition* of
1796+--  `X := Y + 1` with respect to the postcondition `X <= 5`.
1797+
1798+--  Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command `X := Y + 1`
1799+--  with respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as
1800+--  meaning "easiest to satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as
1801+--  many states as possible can satisfy.
1802+
1803+--  `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for postcondition `Q` if
1804+
1805+--  - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
1806+
1807+--  - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is, if
1808+--    `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
1809+
1810+--  Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For example,
1811+--  `Y <= 4` was a weakest precondition above, but so are the logically
1812+--  equivalent assertions `Y < 5`, `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show
1813+--  that any two weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with
1814+--  respect to postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is,
1815+--  `P <<->> P'`.
17841816 
17851817 def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
17861818   ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
1787-  ∀ P' : Assertion, ValidHoareTriple P' c Q → P' ->> P

8--- # Imp: Simple Imperative Programs
9-
10--- In this chapter, we take a more serious look at how to use Lean as a tool
11--- to study other things. Our case study is a *simple imperative programming
12--- language* called Imp, embodying a tiny core fragment of conventional
13--- mainstream languages such as C and Java.
14-
15--- Here is a familiar mathematical function written in Imp.
16-
17---   Z := X;
18---   Y := 1;
19---   while (Z ≠ 0) {
20---     Y := Y * Z;
21---     Z := Z - 1;
22---   }
23-
24--- We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics* of Imp; later
25--- in this volume we develop a theory of *program equivalence* and introduce
26--- *Hoare Logic*, a popular logic for reasoning about imperative programs.
27-
28--- We build Imp in three layers. The first — a core language of *arithmetic
29--- and boolean expressions* — is developed in its own chapter, *Slang*; read
30--- that one first. There you meet the abstract syntax of arithmetic
31--- expressions (`Aexp`) and boolean expressions (`Bexp`), their evaluation
32--- both as a recursive *function* and as an inductive *relation* (proved
33--- equivalent), and a small `optimize0plus` program transformation together
34--- with its correctness proof. Those expressions are *variable-free*.
35-
36--- This chapter picks up from there. First we extend the expressions with
37--- *variables*; then we add a language of *commands* — assignment,
38--- conditionals, sequencing, and loops.
39-
40--- ## Expressions With Variables
41-
42--- Let's return to defining Imp. The next thing we need to do is to enrich our
43--- arithmetic and boolean expressions with variables. To keep things simple,
44--- we'll assume that all variables are global and that they only hold numbers.
45-
46--- ### States
47-
48--- Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their current values,
49--- we'll use total maps from the `Maps` chapter. A *machine state* (or just
50--- *state*) represents the current values of all variables at some point in
51--- the execution of a program.
52-
53--- For simplicity, we assume that the state is defined for *all* variables,
54--- even though any given program is only able to mention a finite number of
55--- them. Because each variable stores a natural number, we represent the state
56--- as a total map from strings (variable names) to `Nat`, and will use `0` as
57--- the default value in the store.
58-
59--- We give the type of variable identifiers a name, `Ident`. For now it is
60--- just `String`; naming it makes the intent clearer.
8+--  # Imp: Simple Imperative Programs
9+
10+--  In this chapter, we take a more serious look at how to use Lean as a
11+--  tool to study other things. Our case study is a *simple imperative
12+--  programming language* called Imp, embodying a tiny core fragment of
13+--  conventional mainstream languages such as C and Java.
14+
15+--  Here is a familiar mathematical function written in Imp.
16+
17+--    Z := X;
18+--    Y := 1;
19+--    while (Z ≠ 0) {
20+--      Y := Y * Z;
21+--      Z := Z - 1;
22+--    }
23+
24+--  We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics* of Imp;
25+--  later in this volume we develop a theory of *program equivalence* and
26+--  introduce *Hoare Logic*, a popular logic for reasoning about imperative
27+--  programs.
28+
29+--  We build Imp in three layers. The first — a core language of
30+--  *arithmetic and boolean expressions* — is developed in its own chapter,
31+--  *Slang*; read that one first. There you meet the abstract syntax of
32+--  arithmetic expressions (`Aexp`) and boolean expressions (`Bexp`), their
33+--  evaluation both as a recursive *function* and as an inductive
34+--  *relation* (proved equivalent), and a small `optimize0plus` program
35+--  transformation together with its correctness proof. Those expressions
36+--  are *variable-free*.
37+
38+--  This chapter picks up from there. First we extend the expressions with
39+--  *variables*; then we add a language of *commands* — assignment,
40+--  conditionals, sequencing, and loops.
41+
42+--  ## Expressions With Variables
43+
44+--  Let's return to defining Imp. The next thing we need to do is to enrich
45+--  our arithmetic and boolean expressions with variables. To keep things
46+--  simple, we'll assume that all variables are global and that they only
47+--  hold numbers.
48+
49+--  ### States
50+
51+--  Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their current values,
52+--  we'll use total maps from the `Maps` chapter. A *machine state* (or
53+--  just *state*) represents the current values of all variables at some
54+--  point in the execution of a program.
55+
56+--  For simplicity, we assume that the state is defined for *all*
57+--  variables, even though any given program is only able to mention a
58+--  finite number of them. Because each variable stores a natural number,
59+--  we represent the state as a total map from strings (variable names) to
60+--  `Nat`, and will use `0` as the default value in the store.
61+
62+--  We give the type of variable identifiers a name, `Ident`. For now it is
63+--  just `String`; naming it makes the intent clearer.
6164 
6265 open scoped MyGetElem
6366 
6467 abbrev Ident := String
6568 abbrev State := TotalMap Ident Nat
6669

100--- ### Notations
101-
102--- To make Imp programs easier to read and write, we introduce some notations.
103-
104--- You do not need to understand exactly what these declarations do. Briefly,
105--- though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:
106-

108---   grammar, called `imp_aexp`. We'll add additional non-terminals further
109---   below.
110-
111--- - Each `syntax` directive defines a grammar production, of which there are
112---   eight in total. The first two define literals, `num` and `ident`, as
113---   `imp_aexp`s. The next several directives define productions for building
114---   larger expressions, with some annotations to define precedence, etc.
115-
116--- - Finally, `macro_rules` is used to translate each production of the
117---   `imp_aexp` nonterminal into a Lean expression.
118-
119--- Boolean expressions and, later, commands follow this same pattern exactly,
120--- so their declarations are collapsed where they appear: open one if you want
121--- to see the pattern repeated, and skip them otherwise.
103+--  ### Notations
104+
105+--  To make Imp programs easier to read and write, we introduce some
106+--  notations.
107+
108+--  You do not need to understand exactly what these declarations do.
109+--  Briefly, though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:
110+
111+--  - The `declare_syntax_cat` directive adds a new non-terminal to Lean's
112+--    grammar, called `imp_aexp`. We'll add additional non-terminals
113+--    further below.
114+
115+--  - Each `syntax` directive defines a grammar production, of which there
116+--    are eight in total. The first two define literals, `num` and `ident`,
117+--    as `imp_aexp`s. The next several directives define productions for
118+--    building larger expressions, with some annotations to define
119+--    precedence, etc.
120+
121+--  - Finally, `macro_rules` is used to translate each production of the
122+--    `imp_aexp` nonterminal into a Lean expression.
123+
124+--  Boolean expressions and, later, commands follow this same pattern
125+--  exactly, so their declarations are collapsed where they appear: open
126+--  one if you want to see the pattern repeated, and skip them otherwise.

204--- ### Delaborators
205-
206--- The notations above are *input* only: they teach Lean how to **read**
207--- `aexp
208--- { … }` and `bexp { … }`, but Lean still **prints** an expression
209--- using its raw constructors -- `example_aexp` shows up as
210--- `Aexp.plus (Aexp.num 3) …` rather than `aexp { 3 + X * 2 }`. A
211--- *delaborator* closes the loop. Where a `macro` turns surface syntax into a
212--- term (*elaboration*), a delaborator does the reverse: it turns an
213--- elaborated term back into surface syntax so that Lean's own output uses our
214--- concrete Imp notation.
215-
216--- Each delaborator walks a term of the given type and rebuilds the matching
217--- piece of `imp_aexp`/`imp_bexp` syntax; a subterm Lean doesn't recognize is
218--- printed with the `~` escape. The `@[delab …]` attribute registers the
219--- top-level function to fire whenever Lean is about to display a term headed
220--- by one of those constructors -- unless notation printing has been switched
221--- off with `set_option pp.notation false`, which lets us fall back to the raw
222--- constructors when debugging (see *Desugaring Notations* below). The
223--- companion *category parenthesizer* re-inserts the parentheses the grammar's
224--- precedences demand, so that, e.g., `(1 + 2) * 3` prints with its
225--- parentheses intact.
226-
227--- You do not need to understand the details, and the code is collapsed below
228--- for that reason. The result is that a `#check`, an `#eval`, or a proof goal
229--- mentioning an Imp expression is displayed in readable Imp syntax rather
230--- than as a pile of constructors.
231-

608--- ### Desugaring Notations
609-
610--- The `imp { … }` notation, together with the delaborators, is purely a
611--- convenience for reading and writing programs. Occasionally, such as when
612--- debugging a definition or a stuck proof, the concrete syntax `hide`s the
613--- underlying structure we want to see. For those moments we can switch the
614--- Imp notation off in Lean's output with `set_option pp.notation false`,
615--- which our delaborators honor.
616-
617--- Note that unlike a `def`, `imp { … }` is a `macro` which is expanded during
618--- elaboration, **before** the resulting term is type-checked. So
619--- `fact_in_lean` is not a program hidden behind a layer of notation that a
620--- proof must first peel back; it simply **is** the underlying tree of `Com`,
621--- `Aexp`, and `Bexp` constructors. Consequently, when a proof goal mentions
622--- an Imp program, tactics such as `cases`, `injection`, and `simp` already
623--- act on those constructors directly -- there is nothing to "unfold". The
624--- delaborators affect only how that tree is **displayed**. Nevertheless,
625--- seeing the raw constructors is sometimes very helpful!

725--- nondeterministic features like `any` to the language, we want the

704+--  In a more conventional functional language like OCaml or Haskell we
705+--  could add the `while` case as follows:

707+--  | .whileDo b c =>

712+--  because the function we want to define is not guaranteed to terminate.
713+--  Indeed, it *doesn't* always terminate: the full `ceval_fun` applied to
714+--  the `loop` program above would run forever. Since Lean aims to be not
715+--  just a programming language but also a consistent logic, any
716+--  potentially non-terminating function must be rejected. Here is what
717+--  would go wrong if Lean allowed non-terminating recursive functions:
718+
719+--  def loop_false (n : Nat) : False := loop_false n
720+
721+--  That is, propositions like `False` would become provable
722+--  (`loop_false 0` would be a proof of `False`), a disaster for logical
723+--  consistency.
724+
725+--  Thus, because it doesn't terminate on all inputs, the full `ceval_fun`
726+--  cannot be written in Lean -- at least not without additional tricks and
727+--  workarounds.
728+
729+--  ### Evaluation as a Relation
730+
731+--  Here's a better way: define `ceval` as a *relation* rather than a
732+--  *function* -- i.e., make its result a `Prop` rather than a `State`,
733+--  similar to what we did for `Aexp.EvalR` in the Slang chapter.
734+
735+--  This is an important change. Besides freeing us from awkward
736+--  workarounds, it gives us more flexibility in the definition. For
737+--  example, if we add nondeterministic features like `any` to the
738+--  language, we want the definition of evaluation to be nondeterministic
739+--  -- i.e., not only will it not be total, it will not even be a function!
740+
741+--  We'll use the notation `st =[ c ]=> st'` for the `Com.EvalR` relation:
742+--  `st =[ c ]=> st'` means that executing program `c` in a starting state
743+--  `st` results in an ending state `st'`. This can be pronounced "`c`
744+--  takes state `st` to `st'`".
745+
746+--  Operational Semantics
747+
748+--  Here is an informal definition of evaluation, presented as inference
749+--  rules for readability:
750+

1055+--  ### Exercise (3 stars): stack_compiler ⭐⭐⭐
1056+
1057+--  Old HP Calculators, programming languages like Forth and Postscript,
1058+--  and abstract machines like the Java Virtual Machine all evaluate
1059+--  arithmetic expressions using a *stack*. For instance, the expression
1060+
1061+--    (2*3)+(3*(4-2))
1062+
1063+--  would be written as
1064+
1065+--          2 3 * 3 4 2 - * +
1066+
1067+--  and evaluated like this (where we show the program being evaluated on
1068+--  the right and the contents of the stack on the left):
1069+
1070+--  [ ]           |    2 3 * 3 4 2 - * +
1071+--        [2]           |    3 * 3 4 2 - * +
1072+--        [3, 2]        |    * 3 4 2 - * +
1073+--        [6]           |    3 4 2 - * +
1074+--        [3, 6]        |    4 2 - * +
1075+--        [4, 3, 6]     |    2 - * +
1076+--        [2, 4, 3, 6]  |    - * +
1077+--        [2, 3, 6]     |    * +
1078+--        [6, 6]        |    +
1079+--        [12]          |
1080+
1081+--  The goal of this exercise is to write a small compiler that translates
1082+--  `aexp`s into stack machine instructions.
1083+
1084+--  The instruction set for our stack language will consist of the
1085+--  following instructions:
1086+
1087+--  - `sPush n`: Push the number `n` on the stack.
1088+
1089+--  - `sLoad x`: Load the identifier `x` from the store and push it on the
1090+--    stack
1091+
1092+--  - `sPlus`: Pop the two top numbers from the stack, add them, and push
1093+--    the result onto the stack.
1094+
1095+--  - `sMinus`: Similar, but subtract the first number from the second.
1096+
1097+--  - `sMult`: Similar, but multiply.
1098+
1099+namespace StackCompiler
1100+
1101+inductive Sinstr : Type where
1102+| sPush (n : Nat)
1103+| sLoad (x : String)
1104+| sPlus
1105+| sMinus
1106+| sMult
1107+
1108+open Sinstr
1109+
1110+--  Write a function to evaluate programs in the stack language. It should
1111+--  take as input a state, a stack represented as a list of numbers (top
1112+--  stack item is the head of the list), and a program represented as a
1113+--  list of instructions, and it should return the stack after executing
1114+--  the program. Test your function on the examples below.
1115+
1116+--  Note that it is unspecified what to do when encountering an `sPlus`,
1117+--  `sMinus`, or `sMult` instruction if the stack contains fewer than two
1118+--  elements. In a sense, it is immaterial what we do, since a correct
1119+--  compiler will never emit such a malformed program. But for sake of
1120+--  later exercises, it would be best to skip the offending instruction and
1121+--  continue with the next one.
1122+

1135+--  Next, write a function that compiles an `Aexp` into a stack machine

1190+--  Imp is rather simple. In a bigger language where evaluating an

1204+--  ### Exercise (3 stars): break_imp (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
1205+
1206+--  Imperative languages like C and Java often include a `break` or similar
1207+--  statement for interrupting the execution of loops. In this exercise we
1208+--  consider how to add `break` to Imp. First, we need to enrich the
1209+--  language of commands with an additional case. Because `break` is a
1210+--  reserved keyword in Lean, we will abbreviate it as `brk`.
1211+
1212+namespace BreakImp
1213+
1214+inductive Com where
1215+  | skip
1216+  | brk                          -- <--- NEW
1217+  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
1218+  | seq (c₁ c₂ : Com)
1219+  | cond (b : Bexp) (c₁ c₂ : Com)
1220+  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
1221+
1222+--  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: commands, macro rules)
1223+
1224+namespace Com
1225+
1226+open Lean in
1227+scoped macro_rules
1228+  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
1229+    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
1230+    else if x.getId == `brk then `(Com.brk)
1231+    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip' or 'break', got '{x.getId}'"
1232+  | `(imp { $c₁; $c₂ }) =>
1233+    `(Com.seq (imp {$c₁}) (imp {$c₂}))
1234+  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
1235+    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
1236+  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c₁} else {$c₂} }) =>
1237+    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c₁}) (imp {$c₂}))
1238+  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
1239+    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
1240+  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
1241+    pure c
1242+
1243+end Com
1244+
1245+open scoped Com
1246+
1247+namespace Delab
1248+open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
1249+
1250+/-- Rebuild `imp_com` syntax from a `BreakImp.Com` term. -/
1251+partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) :=
1252+  delabComInnerFor ``Com do
1253+    let e ← getExpr
1254+    guard <| e.isConstOf ``Com.brk
1255+    annAsTerm (← `(imp_com| $(mkIdent `brk):ident))
1256+
1257+@[delab app.BreakImp.Com.skip, delab app.BreakImp.Com.brk, delab app.BreakImp.Com.asgn,
1258+  delab app.BreakImp.Com.seq, delab app.BreakImp.Com.cond, delab app.BreakImp.Com.whileDo]
1259+partial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1260+  match ← delabComInner with
1261+  | `(imp_com| ~$e) => pure e
1262+  | e => `(term| imp { $e })
1263+
1264+end Delab
1265+
1266+/--
1267+info: imp {
1268+  brk
1269+} : Com
1270+-/
1271+#guard_msgs in
1272+#check imp {brk}
1273+
1274+--  END DETAILS
1275+
1276+--  Next, we need to define the behavior of `brk`. Informally, whenever
1277+--  `brk` is executed in a sequence of commands, it stops the execution of
1278+--  that sequence and signals that the innermost enclosing loop should
1279+--  terminate. (If there aren't any enclosing loops, then the whole program
1280+--  simply terminates.) The final state should be the same as the one in
1281+--  which the `brk` statement was executed.
1282+
1283+--  One important point is what to do when there are multiple loops
1284+--  enclosing a given `brk`. In those cases, `brk` should only terminate
1285+--  the *innermost* loop. Thus, after executing the following...
1286+
1287+--        X := 0;
1288+--        Y := 1;
1289+--        while (0 <> Y) {
1290+--          while (true) {
1291+--            break
1292+--          };
1293+--          X := 1;
1294+--          Y := Y - 1
1295+--        }
1296+
1297+--  ... the value of `X` should be `1`, and not `0`.
1298+
1299+--  One way of expressing this behavior is to add another parameter to the
1300+--  evaluation relation that specifies whether evaluation of a command
1301+--  executes a `brk` statement:
1302+
1303+inductive Result : Type where
1304+  | sContinue
1305+  | sBreak
1306+
1307+open Result
1308+
1309+--  We will use the syntax `st =[ c ]=> st' // s` to mean that, if `c` is
1310+--  started in state `st`, then it terminates in state `st'` and either
1311+--  signals that the innermost surrounding loop (or the whole program)
1312+--  should exit immediately (`s = sBreak`) or that execution should
1313+--  continue normally (`s = sContinue`).
1314+
1315+--  The definition of the `st =[ c ]=> st' // s` relation is very similar
1316+--  to the one we gave above for the regular evaluation relation
1317+--  (`st =[ c ]=> st'`) -- we just need to handle the termination signals
1318+--  appropriately:
1319+
1320+--  - If the command is `skip`, then the state doesn't change and execution
1321+--    of any enclosing loop can continue normally.
1322+
1323+--  - If the command is `brk`, the state stays unchanged but we signal a
1324+--    `sBreak`.
1325+
1326+--  - If the command is an assignment, then we update the binding for that
1327+--    variable in the state accordingly and signal that execution can
1328+--    continue normally.
1329+
1330+--  - If the command is of the form `if (b) {c₁} {c₂}`, then the state is
1331+--    updated as in the original semantics of Imp, except that we also
1332+--    propagate the signal from the execution of whichever branch was
1333+--    taken.
1334+
1335+--  - If the command is a sequence `c₁ ; c₂`, we first execute `c₁`. If
1336+--    this yields a `sBreak`, we skip the execution of `c₂` and propagate
1337+--    the `sBreak` signal to the surrounding context; the resulting state
1338+--    is the same as the one obtained by executing `c₁` alone. Otherwise,
1339+--    we execute `c₂` on the state obtained after executing `c₁`, and
1340+--    propagate the signal generated there.
1341+
1342+--  - Finally, for a loop of the form `while (b) {c}`, the semantics is
1343+--    almost the same as before. The only difference is that, when `b`
1344+--    evaluates to `true`, we execute `c` and check the signal that it
1345+--    raises. If that signal is `sContinue`, then the execution proceeds as
1346+--    in the original semantics. Otherwise, we stop the execution of the
1347+--    loop, and the resulting state is the same as the one resulting from
1348+--    the execution of the current iteration. In either case, since `break`
1349+--    only terminates the innermost loop, `while` signals `sContinue`.
1350+
1351+--  Based on the above description, complete the definition of the
1352+--  `Com.EvalR` relation:
1353+
1354+inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Result → Prop where
1355+  | skip {st : State} : EvalR (imp {skip}) st st sContinue
1356+  -- FILL IN HERE
1357+
1358+scoped notation:40 st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " st1:41 " // " s:41 => Com.EvalR c st0 st1 s
1359+
1360+--  Now prove the following properties of your definition:
1361+
1362+theorem break_ignore (c : Com) (st st' : State) (s : Result) (h : st =[ imp { brk ; ~c } ]=> st' // s) :
1363+  st = st' := by
1364+  sorry
1365+
1366+theorem while_continue (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State) (s : Result)
1367+  (h : st =[ imp { while (~b) {~c} } ]=> st' // s) :
1368+  s = sContinue := by
1369+  sorry
1370+
1371+theorem while_stops_on_break (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State)
1372+  (h₁ : b.eval st = true)
1373+  (h₂ : st =[ imp { ~c } ]=> st' // sBreak) :
1374+  st =[ imp { while (~b) {~c} } ]=> st' // sContinue := by
1375+  sorry
1376+
1377+theorem seq_continue (c₁ c₂ : Com) (st st' st'' : State)
1378+  (h₁ : st =[ imp { ~c₁ } ]=> st' // sContinue)
1379+  (h₂ : st' =[ imp { ~c₂ } ]=> st'' // sContinue) :
1380+  st =[ imp { ~c₁ ; ~c₂ } ]=> st'' // sContinue := by
1381+  sorry
1382+
1383+theorem seq_stops_on_break (c₁ c₂ : Com) (st st' : State)
1384+  (h : st =[ imp { ~c₁ } ]=> st' // sBreak) :
1385+  st =[ imp { ~c₁ ; ~c₂ } ]=> st' // sBreak := by
1386+  sorry
1387+
1388+--  ### Exercise (3 stars): while_break_true (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
1389+
1390+theorem while_break_true (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State)
1391+  (h₁ : st =[ imp { while (~b) {~c} } ]=> st' // sContinue)
1392+  (h₂ : b.eval st' = true) :
1393+  ∃ st'', st'' =[ imp { ~c } ]=> st' // sBreak := by
1394+  sorry
1395+
1396+--  ### Exercise (4 stars): ceval_deterministic (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1397+
1398+theorem ceval_deterministic (c : Com) (st st₁ st₂ : State) (s₁ s₂ : Result)
1399+  (h₁ : st =[ imp { ~c } ]=> st₁ // s₁)
1400+  (h₂ : st =[ imp { ~c } ]=> st₂ // s₂) :
1401+  st₁ = st₂ ∧ s₁ = s₂ := by
1402+  sorry
1403+
1404+end BreakImp
1405+
1406+--  ### Exercise (4 stars): add_for_loop (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1407+
1408+--  Add C-style `for` loops to the language of commands, update the `ceval`
1409+--  definition to define the semantics of `for` loops, and add cases for
1410+--  `for` loops as needed so that all the proofs in this file are accepted
1411+--  by Rocq.
1412+
1413+--  A `for` loop should be parameterized by (a) a statement executed
1414+--  initially, (b) a test that is run on each iteration of the loop to
1415+--  determine whether the loop should continue, (c) a statement executed at
1416+--  the end of each loop iteration, and (d) a statement that makes up the
1417+--  body of the loop. (You don't need to worry about making up a concrete
1418+--  Notation for `for` loops, but feel free to play with this too if you
1419+--  like.)
1420+

3--- # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5--- In **Logical Foundations** (LF) we went through the basics of how to use
6--- Lean to prove theorems and write functional programs. Now, we begin to
7--- shift gears to using it to reason about properties of programs and
8--- programming languages. We begin by looking at a language we call **Slang**
9--- (for *simple language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets us introduce
10--- key concepts for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics* of programming
11--- languages and show how those concepts are realized in Lean.
12-
13--- (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
14--- Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked through
15--- it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next chapter of
16--- this one.)
17-
18--- ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
19-
20--- Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
21--- sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
22-
23--- ### Syntax
3+--  # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4+
5+--  In **Logical Foundations** (LF) we went through the basics of how to
6+--  use Lean to prove theorems and write functional programs. Now, we begin
7+--  to shift gears to using it to reason about properties of programs and
8+--  programming languages. We begin by looking at a language we call
9+--  **Slang** (for *simple language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets
10+--  us introduce key concepts for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics*
11+--  of programming languages and show how those concepts are realized in
12+--  Lean.
13+
14+--  (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
15+--  Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked
16+--  through it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next
17+--  chapter of this one.)
18+
19+--  ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
20+
21+--  Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
22+--  sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
23+
24+--  ### Syntax
2425 
2526 namespace Slang
2627 
27--- These two definitions specify the *abstract syntax* of arithmetic and
28--- boolean expressions.
28+--  These two definitions specify the *abstract syntax* of arithmetic and
29+--  boolean expressions.
2930 
3031 inductive Aexp where
3132   | num (n : Nat)
4243   | not (b : Bexp)
4344   | and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp)
4445 
45--- In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete syntax*
46--- that a programmer would actually write to these abstract syntax trees --
47--- the process that, for example, would translate the string `"1 + 2 * 3"` to
48--- the AST `.plus (.num 1) (.mult (.num 2) (.num 3))`.
49-
50--- For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar
51--- defining the same abstract syntax:
52-
53--- a ::= nat
54---     | a + a
55---     | a − a
56---     | a * a
57--- b ::= bool
58---     | a = a
59---     | a ≠ a
60---     | a ≤ a
61---     | a > a
62---     | ¬ b
63---     | b ∧ b
64-
65--- Compared to the Lean version above...
66-
67--- - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions about
68---   the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the addition
69---   operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other aspects of
70---   lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence of `+`, `-`, and
71---   `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions, etc.) unspecified. Some
72---   additional information -- and human intelligence -- would be required to
73---   turn this description into a formal definition, e.g., for implementing a
74---   compiler. The Lean version consistently omits all this information and
75---   concentrates on the abstract syntax only.

46+--  In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete
47+--  syntax* that a programmer would actually write to these abstract syntax
48+--  trees -- the process that, for example, would translate the string
49+--  `"1 + 2 * 3"` to the AST `.plus (.num 1) (.mult (.num 2) (.num 3))`.
50+
51+--  For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar
52+--  defining the same abstract syntax:
53+
54+--  a ::= nat
55+--      | a + a
56+--      | a − a
57+--      | a * a
58+--  b ::= bool
59+--      | a = a
60+--      | a ≠ a
61+--      | a ≤ a
62+--      | a > a
63+--      | ¬ b
64+--      | b ∧ b
65+
66+--  Compared to the Lean version above...
67+
68+--  - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions
69+--    about the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the
70+--    addition operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other
71+--    aspects of lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence
72+--    of `+`, `-`, and `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions,
73+--    etc.) unspecified. Some additional information -- and human
74+--    intelligence -- would be required to turn this description into a
75+--    formal definition, e.g., for implementing a compiler. The Lean
76+--    version consistently omits all this information and concentrates on
77+--    the abstract syntax only.
78+
79+--  - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its
80+--    informality makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like
81+--    discussions at the blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more
82+--    important than nailing down every detail precisely.
83+
84+--    Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch
85+--    freely among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of
86+--    BNF they're using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready
87+--    informal understanding is all that's important.
88+
89+--  It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones
90+--  for communicating between humans and formal ones for carrying out
91+--  implementations and proofs.

340--- In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for

342--- *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the conclusion
343--- below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be written like

345-

351--- Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version of
352--- the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:

354--- | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
355---         EvalR a₁ n₁ →
356---         EvalR a₂ n₂ →
357---         EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
358-
359--- Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
360--- informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the right
361--- as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks between the
362--- premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as `→`. All the
363--- variables mentioned in the rule (`a₁`, `n₁`, etc.) are implicitly bound by
364--- universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such variables are often called
365--- *metavariables* to distinguish them from the variables of whatever language
366--- we are defining. At the moment, our arithmetic expressions don't include
367--- variables, but we'll soon be adding them.) The whole collection of rules is
368--- understood as being wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In
369--- informal prose, this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let
370--- `Aexp.EvalR` be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
371-
372--- To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single inductive
373--- definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor name; above the
374--- line are the premises, below the line the conclusion; metavariables like
375--- `a₁` and `n₁` are implicitly universally quantified. The whole collection
376--- of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation closed under them:

379---                         num n ⇓ n

381---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁

344+
345+--  In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for

347+--  of *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the
348+--  conclusion below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be
349+--  written like this as an inference rule:
350+
351+--  a₁ ⇓ n₁
352+--                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
353+--                      ------------------          (plus)
354+--                      plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
355+
356+--  Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version
357+--  of the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
358+
359+--  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
360+--          EvalR a₁ n₁ →
361+--          EvalR a₂ n₂ →
362+--          EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
363+
364+--  Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
365+--  informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the
366+--  right as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks
367+--  between the premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as
368+--  `→`. All the variables mentioned in the rule (`a₁`, `n₁`, etc.) are
369+--  implicitly bound by universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such
370+--  variables are often called *metavariables* to distinguish them from the
371+--  variables of whatever language we are defining. At the moment, our
372+--  arithmetic expressions don't include variables, but we'll soon be
373+--  adding them.) The whole collection of rules is understood as being
374+--  wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In informal prose,
375+--  this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let `Aexp.EvalR`
376+--  be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
377+
378+--  To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single
379+--  inductive definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor
380+--  name; above the line are the premises, below the line the conclusion;
381+--  metavariables like `a₁` and `n₁` are implicitly universally quantified.
382+--  The whole collection of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation
383+--  closed under them:
384+
385+--  ---------                (num)
386+--                          num n ⇓ n
387+
388+--                           a₁ ⇓ n₁
389+--                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
390+--                      ------------------           (plus)

572--- At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use by
573--- default?
574-
575--- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
576--- definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable, relational
577--- definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand, and Lean
578--- generates useful inversion and induction principles from them. On the other
579--- hand, functional definitions are automatically deterministic and total --
580--- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these if we need them -- and we
581--- can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify them during proofs.
582-
583--- In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both* styles
584--- plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to switch between
585--- points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
586--- `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.

587+--  On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
588+--  deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove*
589+--  these if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to
590+--  simplify them during proofs.

339+
340+--  The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an instance may

352+--  and `two` to refer to the same term. Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses
353+--  can carry proofs along with data, so we can write the following to
354+--  enforce that `one` and `two` are distinct.

348356 class HasTwo (α : Type) where
349357   one : α
350358   two : α

388--- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to define
389--- mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about how those
390--- operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a
391--- *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
392-
393--- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
394-
395--- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
396---   elements of type `α` into one,
397-
398--- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
399---   element", and
400-
401--- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
402-
403---   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
404---   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is associative)
405-
406--- We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
399+--  This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to
400+--  define mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about
401+--  how those operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a
402+--  typeclass to define a *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that
403+--  includes four things:
404+
405+--  - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
406+
407+--  - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
408+--    elements of type `α` into one,
409+
410+--  - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
411+--    element", and
412+
413+--  - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
414+
415+--    - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
416+
417+--    - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is
418+--      associative)
419+
420+--  We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
407421 
408422 -- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
409423 class OpSet (α : Type) where
417431   right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
418432   assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
419433 
420--- The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass extends the
421--- `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with an operator and some
422--- notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`,
423--- similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.
424-

462--- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
463--- properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on the
464--- typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity element of
465--- a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set with
466--- the same operator, their identity elements must also be the same:
481+--  In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
482+--  properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on
483+--  the typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity
484+--  element of a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the
485+--  same set with the same operator, their identity elements must also be
486+--  the same:
467487 
468488 theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
469489   obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
478498   -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
479499   exact h'
480500

483--- however, because these are class instances instead of normal structures, we
484--- preface our tuple with the `@` symbol. When stepping through the above
485--- proof, if the notation is confusing to you, remember that you can set
486--- `set_option pp.all true` or `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show
487--- you more clearly what is going on. For example, the goal is displayed as
488--- `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit
489--- arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
490--- `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.

501+--  In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances `m₁` and

513+--  A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse* operation
514+--  `inv`, which has the property that `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`.
515+--  We can extend the definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
495516 
496517 class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
497518   inv : α → α
498519   left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
499520   right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id

504--- a group over the integers:

538--- ## Maps
539-
540--- *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in ordinary
541--- programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're going to need
542--- them in many places in later volumes.
543-

560+--  ## Maps
561+
562+--  *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in
563+--  ordinary programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're
564+--  going to need them in many places in later volumes.
565+
566+--  We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a
567+--  "default" element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't
568+--  exist, and *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate
569+--  success or failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps,
570+--  using `none` as the default element.
571+

604+--  ### Total Maps
605+
606+--  The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`,
607+--  with a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs.
608+--  Here, we are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead.
609+--  The advantage of this representation is that it offers a more
610+--  *extensional* view of maps, as we saw with functions in the Logic
611+--  chapter: two maps that respond to every query in the same way will be
612+--  represented as exactly the same function, rather than just as
613+--  "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs that use maps.
614+
615+--  Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them inside a
616+--  `structure` which we call `TotalMap`. Intuitively, a total map just
617+--  contains a function `inner` from a key of type `α` to a value of type
618+--  `β`.

876--- The two remaining facts are equalities *between maps*, so we first need to
877--- say when two maps are equal. Since a total map is implemented as a
878--- function, this is effectively the functional extensionality principle
879--- (`funext`) from the Logic chapter: two maps are equal when they agree at
880--- every key. Recording it once, for maps, and tagging it `@[ext]` lets the
881--- `ext` tactic reduce a goal `m₁ = m₂` to the pointwise one in the proofs

1348+--  Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1349+
1350+--  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):

1366+--  The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1367+--  (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1368+--  number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a
1369+--  terminating mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is
1370+--  true.
1371+
1372+--  This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only
1373+--  by functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false`
1374+--  in finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1375+--  argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether
1376+--  a given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1377+
1378+--  By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1379+--  mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1380+--  contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1381+--  halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this
1382+--  essential difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a
1383+--  boolean, we need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or
1384+--  `false`; this only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1385+
1386+--  The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1387+--  functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly
1388+--  to justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1389+--  required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1390+--  properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property
1391+--  that happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean
1392+--  computation or as a function into Prop.
1393+

1509--- But we have indicated to Lean, using the `noncomputable` keyword and

1513--- of choice to provide a proof that all propositions are *classically*
1514--- decidable. This sort of definition is suitable for use with proofs, but is
1515--- not allowed to be used in conjunction with computational features of Lean
1516--- such as the `decide` tactic or the `#eval` command.
